questions.q: Why is it a problem to write the database password straight into src/server.ts?
questions.explain: Git keeps every old version, so a committed secret stays in the history. Secrets must come from outside the code, usually from environment variables.
options: TypeScript cannot compile strings that contain passwords
Everyone who can read the repository sees it, forever, even after you delete it from the code
The password would be slower to read than an environment variable
It is only a problem in development

questions.q: What is the "twelve-factor" rule for configuration that the lesson follows?
questions.explain: Deploying should never mean changing code. The same build runs on your laptop and in production; only the environment around it differs.
options: Every environment gets its own copy of the code
Configuration is written in a config.ts file per environment
The code is the same everywhere; configuration comes from outside, mostly from environment variables
Configuration must be stored in the database

questions.q: Which of these is configuration?
questions.explain: Configuration is every value that changes between environments. The title rule is the same everywhere, so it is a business rule and stays in the code.
options: The rule that a task title has 3 to 100 characters
The allowed CORS origins, which are http://localhost:5173 on your laptop and https://tasks.example.com in production

questions.q: Two config sources both give port. Which value does the manager use?
questions.explain: The manager merges all sources. For a key given twice, the higher priority wins; keys that only one source gives are kept from that source.
options: The one from the source added first
The one from the source with the higher priority
Neither: it throws a conflict error

questions.q: From lowest to highest priority, what is the usual order of layers?
questions.explain: Defaults are safe values for a developer's computer. The file holds reviewed, non-secret settings. Environment variables are set by whoever runs the app, so they win, and they are the only place for secrets.
options: Defaults in the code, config file, environment variables

questions.q: Why does createEnvironmentConfigSource({ prefix: "TASKS_" }) use a prefix?
questions.explain: The environment is full of unrelated variables. With a prefix, only TASKS_… names are read, and the prefix is removed from the key.
options: So the app only picks up its own variables, not HOME, PATH and everything else in the environment
Because environment variable names must start with a prefix

questions.q: What does failing fast mean for configuration?
questions.explain: Validate the whole configuration at startup. A typo found at 09:00 during deploy is much cheaper than one found at 12:00 by a user.
options: The app starts as quickly as possible and checks settings later
A wrong setting stops the app when it starts, with a clear message, instead of failing hours later when a request uses it
The app retries loading the config until it works
The app ignores bad settings and uses defaults

questions.q: Why does the config schema use schema.coerce.number() for port?
questions.explain: A plain number schema would refuse the string "8080". coerce converts it first, then the checks (int, min, max) run on the number.
options: Environment values are strings; coerce turns "8080" into 8080 and refuses "80x"
To make the port a string

questions.q: Where should the Task API's jwt_secret come from?
questions.explain: Secrets never live in code or in a committed file. They come from the environment, which whoever runs the app controls.
options: A default in the code, such as "change-me"
Only from the environment (or a secrets manager that sets it)
A query parameter on the first request

questions.q: Why must a missing secret stop the app instead of falling back to a default like "change-me"?
questions.explain: If production quietly uses "change-me", everyone who has read the code knows your signing key. Refusing to start is the safe answer.
options: A default secret is written in the code, so it is a public secret: anyone could sign valid tokens with it
Because the schema cannot have defaults
It should not; a default is fine in production

questions.q: You want to log the loaded configuration at startup. Which is right?
questions.explain: toObject() returns the real values, secrets included. toSafeObject() replaces sensitive values with "[REDACTED]". Never log the whole process.env.
options: console.log(config.toSafeObject()), or better, only the few settings you need

questions.q: A teammate stores an API key as TASKS_NOTE. What happens in toSafeObject()?
questions.explain: Both the config manager and the logger look at names such as secret, password, token, api_key. Give secrets obvious names, like TASKS_API_KEY.
options: It is redacted, because the value looks random
It is shown in full: redaction recognises secrets by their key name, and note looks innocent
It is removed from the object
The config manager refuses to load

questions.q: You find that the JWT secret was printed in production logs last week. What should you do?
questions.explain: Logs are copied to many places and kept for months. Once a secret has been logged, you cannot know who read it, so it must be replaced.
options: Delete the log lines; then it is safe again
Treat it as leaked: replace the secret, and fix the code that logged it
Make the secret longer by adding characters to the old one

questions.q: Why does loadConfig build its error message from setting names and schema messages, never from the values?
questions.explain: An error message usually ends up in a log. "jwt_secret: String must be at least 32 characters" tells you what to fix without showing the secret.
options: Because values are always too long
So even a wrong secret cannot leak into the logs through the error message
Because the schema does not know the values
So the message can be translated

questions.q: NODE_ENV is not set. What does resolveEnvironment() from @zudojs/constants return?
questions.explain: With no NODE_ENV, you get "development". Production must be switched on on purpose, and then the stricter rules apply.

questions.q: What is the right way to handle a .env file for development?
questions.explain: .env may hold real passwords, so it is never committed. .env.example shows which variables exist, so a new developer knows what to set. For a script that does not load it itself, node --env-file=.env does the same job.
options: Commit it, so every developer has the same values
Let the app load it (the generated loadConfig reads .env for you), keep it out of git (.gitignore), and commit a .env.example with no real values
Use it in production instead of real environment variables

questions.q: In development the Task API's host defaults to 127.0.0.1, in production to 0.0.0.0. Why?
questions.explain: 0.0.0.0 listens on every network interface, so anyone on the same Wi-Fi could reach your dev server. In production the server must be reachable, so it uses 0.0.0.0.
options: 127.0.0.1 only accepts connections from your own computer, which is safer on a laptop in a café
Production servers cannot use 127.0.0.1 for HTTPS

questions.q: loadConfig() throws a ConfigurationError in src/server.ts. What does the lesson do?
questions.explain: The message already says what to fix, so a stack trace adds nothing. Exit code 1 tells the platform the start failed.
options: Start the server anyway with defaults
Print the full stack trace and keep running
Print Cannot start: … with the message and exit with code 1
Retry every second until the config is valid

questions.explain: The override's higher priority wins for port. Keys the override did not mention keep their defaults.

questions.explain: get() gives undefined for a missing key, an accessor uses its fallback, and required() throws.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: HOME does not start with TASKS_, so it is ignored. The prefix is removed, names are lower-cased, and __ becomes a dot.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every value from the environment is a string. The typed accessor number() converts it, so adding 1 does arithmetic instead of joining text.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: get("debug") is the string "false", which is truthy. boolean("debug") converts it to the real false.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: port comes from the defaults, host from the file (priority 10 beats the defaults), and rate_limit_max from the environment (priority 20 beats both).

questions.q: The config file does not exist. What does this print?
questions.explain: An optional source that fails is skipped, so the app still starts with the other layers.
options: ENOENT: no such file or directory

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toSafeObject() is the copy for logs: the secret-looking key is redacted. The accessors still give your code the real value, which is 32 characters long.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Redaction works on key names. api_key is on the list of sensitive names; note is not, so a secret stored there is shown in full.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: schema.coerce.number() turns the string "8080" into the number 8080 before checking it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: All the problems are reported at once, each with the setting's name. "80x" cannot become a number; "0" becomes 0, which is below the minimum.
options:
port: Cannot coerce string to number
rate_limit_max: Expected >= 1, received 0
port: Cannot coerce string to number

port: Expected number, received string
rate_limit_max: Expected number, received string

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The environment gives one comma-separated string. The transform splits it, trims each origin, and drops empty pieces, so a trailing comma or an empty value gives no bogus origin.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: .optional() allows the key to be missing (in development). If it is given, it must still have at least 32 characters, so the short "secret" fails.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: resolveEnvironment reads NODE_ENV. When it is not set, you get "development".
questions.code:
import { resolveEnvironment } from "@zudojs/constants";

console.log(resolveEnvironment({}), resolveEnvironment({ NODE_ENV: "production" }), resolveEnvironment({ NODE_ENV: "test" }));

questions.q: Create a config manager with two sources: defaults { port: 3000 }, and an environment source with prefix TASKS_, env: fakeEnv and priority 50. Load it and assign it to config. The program should print 8080 number.
questions.explain: The environment source has the higher priority, so its "8080" wins over the default. number() converts the string to a number.

questions.q: The startup line below logs the real secret. Change it so the log shows the redacted copy instead. The program should print config: { port: '8080', jwt_secret: '[REDACTED]' }.
questions.explain: toObject() gives the real values; toSafeObject() is the copy for logs. A secret that reaches a log must be treated as leaked.

questions.q: Add a custom source for the file values with createCustomConfigSource("file", loader, { priority: 10 }). The loader returns { values: fileValues, source: "config.json", type: ConfigSourceType.FILE }. The program should print 3000 0.0.0.0.
questions.explain: A custom source is a loader function plus a priority. In a real app the loader reads and parses config.json; the file's host beats the default, and port keeps its default.

questions.q: Finish parseOrigins: split the comma-separated text, trim each origin, and drop empty pieces. The program should print [ 'http://localhost:5173', 'https://tasks.example.com' ] and then [].
questions.explain: Without the filter, the trailing comma (or an empty setting) would add an empty origin to the allow-list. This is the same logic as the schema's transform.

questions.q: Write ConfigSchema with two keys: port, a whole number from 0 to 65535, and rate_limit_max, a whole number from 1 to 10000. Both arrive as strings, so use schema.coerce.number(). The program should print true 8080 300 and then false.
questions.explain: coerce turns the strings into numbers first; .int().min().max() then check them. Port 70000 is too big, so the second parse fails.

questions.q: Finish describeIssues: when the parse failed, return one string path: message per issue, joined with "; ". Use issue.path.join(".") for the path, and never include the value. The program should print port: Cannot coerce string to number.
questions.explain: safeParse returns the issues instead of throwing. Each issue has a path and a message, which say what to fix without printing the value, so a wrong secret can never leak through this message.
questions.expected: port: Cannot coerce string to number

questions.q: Finish checkProduction: when config.production is true and config.jwt_secret is undefined, throw a ConfigurationError with the message TASKS_JWT_SECRET must be set in production. Otherwise return "ok". The program should print ok, ConfigurationError: TASKS_JWT_SECRET must be set in production, and ok.
questions.explain: Development may run without the secret until login exists. Production refuses to start, and the message names the variable without showing any value. Never fall back to a default secret.
questions.expected:
ok
ConfigurationError: TASKS_JWT_SECRET must be set in production
ok

questions.q: Add a request_timeout_ms key to the schema: coerced to a number, a whole number from 1000 to 120000. The program should print 500 -> false and 5000 -> true.
questions.explain: The environment value beats the default, arrives as a string, and coerce converts it. 500 is below the minimum, so the configuration is refused at startup.
